What should happen to sale s4?

We want to enrich sales with product categories.For example, B1 links a sale to books. The lookup has one row per product_id.

Sale s4 exists, but its product M1 is missing from the lookup.Pause: should we omit the sale, or keep it without a category?

INNER keeps only sales with a matching product.s4 is absent from the result. The source sales data is unchanged.

LEFT keeps every sale, including s4.Only the missing product category becomes NULL. Next, watch these same five sales pass through both rules.

Danny’s Code Corner1
Establish the business task before the metaphor: sales records need categories from a product lookup. Read the three sales fields and the two product fields. Each product ID is unique in this lookup. B1 maps to books; G1 maps to games. Reveal the unmatched M1 sale and ask the audience what should happen to it. INNER omits it from output; LEFT retains all its original values and supplies NULL for category. These exact records become boats on the next slide; the boats represent rows, not Spark's physical execution.

Same five sales. One unique product lookup.

Now bring all five sales to the same lookup.The lookup has unique product IDs. Four sales can find a product; M1 cannot.

The matching condition is product_id equality.B1 gets books and G1 gets games. M1 has no matching product row.

LEFT keeps every sale in this example.All five rows remain, totalling 100. M1 has a NULL category.

Danny’s Code Corner2
Carry the same s4/M1/10 boat from the close-up. One canal, two alternative runs: do not imply the output splits simultaneously into inner and left. Next runs INNER; next rewinds the same inputs and runs LEFT. Join choice changes the population of your dataset: totals 90 versus 100 are analytically consequential. This left join preserves five rows because right keys are unique; duplicate matches are explored later. Ordering and sequential boat movement are illustrative, not actual Spark execution. Input data is never deleted.

sales.join(products, "product_id", "inner")sales.join(products, "product_id", "left")

A join produces matching row pairs.Here the product lookup has one row per key, so each sale has at most one match.

INNER requires a matching product.s4 / M1 is omitted from the result; the other four sales acquire their categories.

LEFT retains s4 / M1 and sets category to NULL.KEEP describes the row. NULL describes its missing right-side value.

Danny’s Code Corner3
End by asking: we know which rows belong together, but what if they live on different machines? Transition directly to shuffle and then skew. Explicitly remove the metaphor. Sale IDs s1–s5 and all amounts are unchanged from the boats. KEEP is an explanation of retention, not a literal output column; product category is the value added by the join. For a USING-style join on product_id, only one key column remains. Unique right keys are critical to these counts. Ordinary equality and missing matches shown; NULL keys, duplicate keys and semi/anti are later topics. Input setup remains joins-example.py. Official reference: https://spark.apache.org/docs/latest/sql-ref-syntax-qry-select-join.html

sales.join(products, "product_id", "left_semi")sales.join(products, "product_id", "left_anti")

Semi answers “is there a match?”Keep the matching sales, without adding product columns or multiplying them by right-side duplicates.

Anti answers “which sales have no match?”This is a useful reconciliation check before trusting an enrichment join.

Danny’s Code Corner4
Semi and anti return only the left columns. Semi preserves left-side duplicates, but matching duplicates on the right do not multiply the output. Anti is useful for coverage checks. Null keys do not match under ordinary equality; a null left key is retained by anti for this ordinary equi-join. Do not equate this mechanically with SQL NOT IN and its null semantics. Source: https://spark.apache.org/docs/latest/sql-ref-syntax-qry-select-join.html

What does it take
to get this record there?

CPUPartitioning and serialization
Disk I/OWriting and reading shuffle blocks
Network I/OFetching blocks held remotely

Follow B1 / 10 along the Worker C → Worker A arrow.We have chosen one remote transfer from the diagram you just saw.

The source has to prepare and store the data for its destinations.Even before matching rows, Spark has partitioned, serialized and written shuffle data.

The destination fetches its blocks, then reads and decodes the records.At scale, the bytes written, read and transferred compete for finite disk and network bandwidth.

The join task can now match this sale with its product.The cost depends on how much data must move, how it is processed, and how evenly the work is spread.

Danny’s Code Corner5
Optional reference close-up for the main chapter’s shuffle lesson. Return to the chapter using the link beside Replay. Keep the audience on the exact B1 sale with amount10 from Worker C, going to the join task on Worker A. Do not introduce new data or a benchmark. 1. “Let’s open just one of those arrows.” 2. The source task assigns records to destination partitions, encodes them, and writes intermediate shuffle output. A block contains records for one destination; the pictured B1 sale is one representative record, not a separate network request or file per row. Batches/blocks are transferred. 3. The downstream task fetches the blocks for its partition from their source locations, then reads and deserializes the data. The remote part crosses the network; local blocks do not. Explain WHY this costs time: extra passes over data, CPU for encoding/decoding, storage I/O and network transfer. Larger volumes compete for finite bandwidth and can add memory pressure; sorting or hashing inside the local join contributes additional work. The transfer arrow is not a fixed-duration timeline, and the picture does not model concurrent pipelining. 4. The selected sale is matched with B1/books, giving B1/10/books. The other B1 records and product record come from the preceding diagram. Do not say all cluster tasks must wait until every transfer in the cluster has finished. This is the conventional Spark shuffle with worker-local shuffle storage; it is not another Parquet/HDFS source scan. Input caching does not remove a required exchange. Implementations with remote shuffle services differ. A compatible existing distribution or a broadcast strategy may avoid the illustrated exchanges. Partial aggregation can reduce the records/bytes sent for suitable aggregate functions. This is not a claim that grouping must transfer every raw row. End with: “Now we can compare strategies by asking what they move and what they do once it arrives. Then: what happens if one destination receives most of it?” Continue into sort-merge and shuffled hash; broadcast changes how matching data is made available, and the existing skew lesson shows the long tail. Sources: https://spark.apache.org/docs/latest/rdd-programming-guide.html#shuffle-operations ; https://spark.apache.org/docs/latest/sql-performance-tuning.html .
